description: We are a team from Systems and Mechanical Engineering passionate about space exploration and video games. We bring logic, programming, and technical design skills to create a 3D game where players can design and simulate space missions. We seek creative, committed people eager to learn. Join us to share your ideas and build an educational, interactive experience. No programming experience is needed: we value teamwork and initiative.
summary:
Project Summary: Expedition EM-4X

"Expedition EM-4X" is a "Lessons Learned Engine" designed to transform the frustration of failure into transferable knowledge. More than a flight simulator, it recreates celebrated NASA missions to demonstrate that answering profound scientific questions, such as discovering new materials (Lonsdaleite), is the true driving force of space exploration.

The project addresses the challenge by abstracting the complex mathematics of aerospace engineering behind interactive decision-making. Users assume multiple roles and configure interdependent components to design rockets, confronting real emergencies and the unforgiving uncertainty of missions with no second chances. Players will experience authentic technical failures—such as excessive aerodynamic pressure (Max-Q), trajectory misalignment, propellant imbalances, or communications resonance locks—forcing them to learn how to overcome these hurdles.

This platform is important because it proves to the public that a "game-over" is not the end, but merely one of millions of necessary errors required to achieve success, honoring NASA's true iterative philosophy. By simulating every step of a scientific expedition, the project demonstrates that advancing toward tomorrow means evolving by actively learning from the past.
details:
Project Details: Expedition EM-4X

What does it do or how does it work? Expedition EM-4X is an interactive 3D simulator that puts players in the role of space systems engineers. It works by guiding the user through the four official mission segments (Launch, Space, Ground, and User), directly applying NASA's Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1-4). The player designs the spacecraft by configuring multiple components, balancing critical resources (mass, power, ∆v, and a baseline budget of $100M USD), and executing the flight while confronting the unforgiving laws of orbital physics.

What are its benefits? It abstracts the mathematical complexity of aerospace engineering behind intuitive visual and interactive decisions, making mission design accessible to the general public. It teaches that space travel extends far beyond the spectacle of launch; the true benefit lies in answering profound scientific questions, such as the discovery and investigation of new materials (e.g., Lonsdaleite).

What is the anticipated impact of the project? To demonstrate that advancing toward tomorrow is synonymous with evolving by learning from the past. The project aims to shift the public perception of failure: a "game-over" in the simulation is not the end, but rather one of millions of necessary errors required to achieve success, thereby honoring the true iterative philosophy of the space agency.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Engine & Core Logic: Unity 6 and C# for 3D physical simulation, trajectory calculations, and resource balancing (mass, power, and budget).
  • Frontend & Interface: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to design a 2.5D tactical HUD interface overlaid on the 3D canvas.
  • Cloud Deployment (Hardware/Software): WebGL build hosted on Vercel via GitHub, enabling 100% execution within the client's web browser.
  • NASA Theoretical Frameworks: Integration of data architecture from the General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT), Mission Design Lab (MDL), and JPL's CML frameworks.

How is your project creative? Its creativity lies in its conceptualization as an "Engine of Lessons Learned." Instead of offering an idealized, arcade-style space flight, the creative core relies on deliberately simulating the frustration of real technical aerospace failures—such as excessive aerodynamic pressure at Max-Q, trajectory vector misalignment, or communications resonance locks—and transforming that frustration into transferable knowledge for the player.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Hardware Accessibility: The project was aggressively optimized to lower the minimum requirements to just 4 GB of RAM and 0 MB of local storage, ensuring the game runs smoothly in school environments or on basic hardware via web browsers.
  • Regulatory Compliance & Data Sovereignty: We ensured that all infrastructure, repositories (GitHub), and cloud services (Vercel) operate strictly within U.S. servers. We exclusively used open-source libraries and official data (NASA, CSA), completely eliminating dependencies on servers or APIs from restricted countries.
  • Multidisciplinary Operation: We factored in collaborative human-in-the-loop dynamics by dividing responsibilities across Science, Engineering, Launch, and Communications. This structure accurately simulates operational uncertainty and forces compromise in scenarios where second chances do not exist.
